title: The Kieninger Trap
subtitle: Budapest Gambit — the discovered pin and the knight on d3
summary: The most beautiful trap in the 1.d4 repertoire: in the Budapest Gambit, a knight recaptures on e5 and quietly becomes the lid on a box. When White wins Black's bishop with a pawn, the knight hops to d3 — checkmate, with the e2-pawn frozen by a pin that did not exist one move earlier. A masterclass in discovered pins and blind captures.

metadata.historicalContext: Named for the German International Master Georg Kieninger, who sprang it against Godai at Vienna 1925. It remains the Budapest Gambit's crown jewel and a fixture of every tactics anthology since — few mates use the victim's own army so completely.

rootAnnotations.title: What this trap teaches
rootAnnotations.body: Two deep ideas hide in this miniature. First, the discovered pin: a piece moving off a line can create a pin that freezes a defender the same instant an attack needs it frozen. Second, the blind recapture: 'I take because he took' is not a move — it is the absence of one. The final position, where five White units imprison their own king, is the standing monument to both.

annotations.title: The setup — the Budapest Gambit
annotations.body: Black offers a center pawn on move two for rapid piece play against d4 and e5. A respectable surprise weapon rather than a refuted stunt: White keeps a small edge with care — the operative word in everything that follows.
The knight chases the pawn it just gambited — Black intends to regain it with pieces, arriving fast on the squares around White's king while doing so.
White holds the extra pawn the principled way, with a developing move. Perfectly sound — the danger in this variation is never White's setup, only a capture White will be offered four moves from now.
A check that pulls a White piece to a passive blocking square — and, as it turns out, begins measuring White's king for a very small room.

Blocking with the knight keeps the structure tidy — and places a White piece on d2, the king's only future flight square. No one notices such details until move eight. Chess tragedies are built from furniture arranged this innocently.

annotations.title: The quiet gun on the e-file
annotations.body: The queen renews pressure on e5 — that is her day job. Her secret job: she now stands on the e-file, aimed through e5 at the pawn on e2 and the king behind it. For the moment two knights' worth of traffic blocks the view. Remember this queen; the entire mate is her doing, and she will never move again.

White puts the question to the bishop — playable, but it hands Black a forcing sequence. Before advancing: Black now regains the e5-pawn with a knight capture. After the dust settles, which White pawn will be pinned, and by whom?

annotations.title: The temptation is served
annotations.body: Black regains the gambit pawn and appears to have simply forgotten the attacked bishop on b4 — a whole piece, free, protected by nothing. The offer is the trap: White's correct move is to capture on e5 with the knight first (see the variation), trading pieces before collecting the bishop. The greedy order loses to a detail sitting in plain sight on the e-file.

annotations.title: The trigger — the blind capture
annotations.body: 'He left the bishop, I take the bishop.' But look at what the position became while White was counting material: Black's knight on e5 is a lid about to lift off the e-file, White's king has exactly one flight square — d2, occupied by his own knight since move six — and d1 belongs to his own queen. The box was assembled piece by piece; this capture declines the last chance to not close it.

annotations.title: The avoidance — capture in the right order
annotations.body: White trades knights immediately. After Black recaptures, the e-file is blocked by Black's own knight, the d3 mating square is covered, and only then does White safely consider axb4 — the bishop was never running anywhere. Move order inside a combination matters as much as the moves: when two captures are available, calculate both sequences, not just both captures.

annotations.title: The punishment — mate by discovered pin
annotations.body: The knight steps off the e-file to deliver check, and its departure is the whole genius: the e7-queen's frozen line to e2 opens the same instant, pinning the e2-pawn — so exd3, the one move that refutes everything, is illegal. Now count the king's room: d1 is his own queen, d2 his own knight, f1 his own bishop, f2 his own pawn. Five White units, every one a wall. Checkmate with almost all of Black's army still at home.

annotations.title: What you should have noticed
annotations.body: Three lessons: pins can be created by a departure — when your piece leaves a line, ask what now shoots down it, in both directions; recaptures are decisions, and the reflex 'take back' is where combinations hide (the Légal, Elephant, and Lasker traps all bill the same reflex); and count your king's flight squares whenever the opponent's pieces gather near it — a full, healthy army can be checkmated the moment it becomes its own prison. That is the Kieninger's immortal image.
